n: Paul compares God’s people before Christ to an underage heir: though he will own everything, while a child he has no more freedom than a servant.

f.g: In Roman law a minor heir was under guardians until a set age.

n: He is under guardians and managers until the date his father has set.
Likewise, before Christ, we were like children enslaved to the basic principles of this world.

f.g: Basic principles or elementary rules — possibly also spiritual forces.

n: But at exactly the right time, God sent His Son, born of a woman and born under the law — fully human, fully subject to the law.
He came to redeem those under the law, so we could be adopted as God’s sons and daughters with full rights.
Because they are His children, God sent the Spirit of His Son into their hearts, crying, “Abba, Father!” — an intimate Aramaic word for father.

f.g: Aramaic for “father,” used by children in close, loving address.

n: So you are no longer a slave but a child — and if a child, then an heir of God through Christ.
Before knowing God, these Gentiles served beings that are not truly gods.
Now that they know God — or rather are known by Him — why go back to weak, worthless principles and be enslaved again?
They were carefully observing special days, months, seasons, and years — perhaps Jewish festival calendars imposed as requirements for salvation.

f.w: days, and months, and times, and years

n: Paul fears his work among them may have been wasted.
He pleads: become free like me, because I became like you Gentiles. You didn’t wrong me before.

f.g: Free from the law as a means of justification.

n: They remember that it was because of an illness that Paul first preached to them.

f.g: A physical illness, possibly connected to his “thorn in the flesh.”

n: Though his condition was a trial to them, they didn’t despise him but welcomed him as an angel — even as Christ Jesus.

f.w: my temptation which was in my flesh
f.g: His physical condition, which tested them.

n: What happened to their joy? They would have torn out their own eyes for him — which some take as a hint that Paul’s illness affected his eyes.

f.g: Possibly a hint of an eye problem; or simply an expression of devotion.

n: Has he become their enemy for telling them the truth?

f.w: because I tell you the truth

n: The false teachers court them eagerly, but not for good. They want to shut them out from Paul so they’ll be devoted to them instead.
It is good to be eagerly sought for good purposes, at all times — not just while Paul is present.
Paul feels like a mother in labor again for them, until Christ is fully formed in them.

f.w: until Christ be formed in you

n: He wishes he could be with them to speak in a gentler tone, because he is perplexed about them.
To those wanting to be under the law: do you actually listen to what the law (the books of Moses) says?

f.g: Here, the Torah — the five books of Moses.

n: Genesis says Abraham had two sons: Ishmael by Hagar, a servant woman, and Isaac by Sarah, a free woman.
Ishmael was born in the ordinary way; Isaac was born because of God’s promise.
Paul treats this as an allegory of two covenants. Hagar represents the covenant from Mount Sinai, whose children are born into bondage.

f.g: A story used to illustrate a spiritual truth.

n: Hagar stands for Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the earthly Jerusalem of Paul’s day, in bondage with her children under the law.
But the heavenly Jerusalem is free, and she is our mother.
Paul quotes Isaiah: the barren woman will rejoice, for she will have more children than the married one — a promise of a vast family through grace.
Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise.
As Ishmael mocked Isaac, so now those born of the flesh persecute those born of the Spirit.
Scripture says: “Cast out the slave woman and her son,” for he won’t share the inheritance with the free woman’s son.

f.w: Cast out the bondwoman and her son

n: So believers are children not of slavery but of freedom.
